drapeaux.note: Citation originally in French, by Jean-Jacques Rousseau (Les Confessions, Book VI); retranslated from the French. A public-domain English translation of Book VI exists (London, Aldus Society, 1903; Project Gutenberg #3906, https://www.gutenberg.org/ebooks/3906), but it reads "the thoughtless saying of a great princess, who, on being informed that the country people had no bread, replied, 'Then let them eat pastry!'", rendering pis-aller as "thoughtless saying" and brioche as "pastry", with no counterpart to "I bought brioche". It was not substituted because the entry's argument rests on "brioche" and on the sense of a stopgap.

Quotations originally in French, retranslated from the French: Rousseau (Confessions, Book VI, the princess and the brioche), Alphonse Karr (Les Guêpes, 1841 and 1843), Madame de Boigne (Mémoires, remark attributed to Madame Victoire).

titre: Marie-Antoinette's Brioche, a Line Older Than She Is
accroche: Rousseau tells the brioche anecdote in his Confessions, written in 1765, five years before Marie-Antoinette arrived in France.
contenu_vulgarise:
In 1765, Jean-Jacques Rousseau writes the first six books of his *Confessions* (*The Confessions*), which will not be published until 1782. In Book VI, he tells a memory from his youth, at the home of M. de Mably, whose children he tutors. He has developed a taste for a little white wine from Arbois, procures a few bottles from time to time to drink in private, but he "could never drink without eating." He needs bread, and he dares neither to have the footmen buy it nor to go to a baker himself: could a fine gentleman with a sword at his side go into a bakery to buy a piece of bread? "Finally I remembered the stopgap of a great princess who was told that the peasants had no bread, and who replied: Let them eat brioche. I bought brioche." The anecdote is nothing like a lampoon: it is an image of compromise, not an attack on a queen. Rousseau names no one, and English Wikipedia adds that he may have invented it.

## A Line Written Before Its Accused Arrived

Here is the chronological problem. Marie-Antoinette, born in 1755, does not arrive in France, from Austria, until 1770, to marry the future Louis XVI. Yet in 1765, Rousseau has already written this passage: the archduchess is nine years old and still lives in Austria. She cannot possibly be the "great princess" whose remark Rousseau reports. The earliest association between this line and Marie-Antoinette appears nearly half a century after the queen's death (1793), from the pen of the journalist Alphonse Karr, in his periodical *Les Guêpes* (*The Wasps*): in November 1841, he reports it cautiously, as a saying "true or false" attributed to the queen; in 1843, far from asserting it, he calls it into question even more deeply, having found in a book from 1760 (before Marie-Antoinette's arrival in France, that is) an almost identical line attributed to a duchess of Tuscany, which seems to him "to roughly prove that the saying was not said by Marie-Antoinette, but found again and put into circulation against her."

## A Line That Has Been Changing Addressees for More Than Two Centuries

What is most interesting is not that the line is false, but that it keeps changing owners. The duchess of Tuscany found by Karr is not the only other candidate: the memoirs of Madame de Boigne, for their part, report a similar version, about pâté crust rather than brioche, attributed to Madame Victoire, daughter of Louis XV: "But good heavens, if only they could resign themselves to eating pâté crust!" Wikipedia also mentions a Chinese emperor of the 3rd century, Jin Huidi, to whom a remark is attributed, in front of a people without rice: "Why do they not eat meat?" The motif (a powerful person suggesting, without grasping the destitution, a food they believe common to people who have no bread) thus circulates from one figure to another, before and after Marie-Antoinette.

Marie-Antoinette therefore did not invent the indifference of the powerful to bread that is missing: she inherited a line that was already circulating before her, and the image of a queen cut off from the people gave it its most convenient and most lasting home.

carte.punch: Rousseau writes the brioche line five years before Marie-Antoinette arrives in France.
carte.idee: “Let them eat brioche” comes from Rousseau's Confessions, whose first six books were written in 1765. Marie-Antoinette does not arrive in France until 1770. The association with the queen first appears, with doubt, in a periodical in 1841, and its author calls it into question in 1843.

quiz.question: Why can the line “Let them eat brioche” not be Marie-Antoinette's?
choix: Because it is written in German in the original text
Because Rousseau wrote it before Marie-Antoinette arrived in France
Because the line comes from a speech given in the Assembly
quiz.explication: Rousseau writes the first six books of the Confessions in 1765, when Marie-Antoinette, born in 1755, is nine years old and still living in Austria: she does not arrive in France until 1770. Nothing points to a German version, an aversion to brioche, or a parliamentary origin: the association with the queen appears in a press article from 1841, with doubt, and its author himself calls it into question in 1843.

quiz_supplementaire.question: According to Madame de Boigne's memoirs, what similar version of the line circulates, and attributed to whom?
choix: About white bread, attributed to the Duchess of Tuscany
About table wine, attributed to Rousseau himself
About pâté crust, attributed to Madame Victoire, daughter of Louis XV
About pastries, attributed to Louis XV himself
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Madame de Boigne's memoirs report the remark not about brioche but about pâté crust, attributing it to Madame Victoire, daughter of Louis XV, and not to Marie-Antoinette.

quiz_supplementaire.question: When does Alphonse Karr first associate the brioche line with Marie-Antoinette, and with what caution?
choix: In November 1841, in Les Guêpes, as a saying that may be true or false
In 1843, in Les Guêpes, asserting it without reservation
In 1770, at Marie-Antoinette's arrival in France, as an established fact
In 1793, in a pamphlet published after the queen's death
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Karr first reports the saying in November 1841 in Les Guêpes, presenting it with caution as a saying that may be true or false, not as an established fact.

quiz_supplementaire.question: Why does Rousseau say he bought brioche, in the anecdote in Book VI of the Confessions?
choix: He wanted to give a gift to his pupils, M. de Mably's children
He lacked bread to go with a little white wine and did not dare go into a bakery
He had been told by the queen to hand out brioche to the peasants
He had been fasting for several days for lack of money and had only brioche left
quiz_supplementaire.explication: Rousseau says he liked drinking a little white wine from Arbois but could not drink without eating; not daring to have the footmen buy bread or to go into a bakery himself, he recalls the great princess's remark and buys brioche.
